Three Indexes

A story read three ways at once.

MOTIF  the smallest element that survives retelling
FUNCTION  the slot it occupies in the sequence
TYPE  the whole tale it is a version of

MATCH runs entirely in this page — no network, no model, same answer every time. READ sends the text to a model instead.

READ needs an Anthropic API key when this file is opened from your own disk. It stays in this tab and is never saved anywhere.

The Index

Everything this instrument is able to recognize. Follow a motif to the tales that carry it, or a tale to the motifs it is made of.

Provenance

The tales are common inheritance; the finding aid is not. This index was rebuilt from open sources, and every field in it records which source supplied it, so nothing here is something you have to take on trust.

where the numbers came from

The sources, with their licences as I found them:

  • Wikidata — CC0; supplied 45,512 motif glosses, motif lists for 98 tale types
  • University of Missouri ATU–AT–Motif concordance — library guide; facts transcribed from the indexes; supplied 2 motif glosses, motif lists for 867 tale types
  • Nakawake & Sato 2019 supplementary data — none declared; derived from Uther 2004 — structure only, excludable; supplied motif lists for 292 tale types
  • Multilingual Folk Tale Database via Internet Archive — tale texts not redistributed; only derived term counts kept; supplied typical vocabulary for 106 tale types
  • Original glosses written for this index — original text; supplied 4 motif glosses

This build holds 45,518 motifs (45,518 with a gloss) and 1,553 tale types, 1,547 titled and 978 with a motif list. 2,096 motifs are tied to at least one type; the rest are catalogued but not yet linked to a tale. The index is strongest where the concordances are — tales of magic and animal tales — and thin elsewhere.

Two things worth knowing. First, Thompson's 1955–58 Motif-Index is still in copyright. Wikidata's motif labels are released CC0, but they carry Thompson's wording, so the gloss on most motifs here is his phrasing as Wikidata's volunteers transcribed it; the structure (codes, hierarchy, which types use which motifs) is the part this instrument is really built on. The handful of glosses marked original were written for this index. Second, source errors that could be proven were corrected and are marked where they occur — for instance a repeated final segment, B11.11.11 for B11.11, is repaired only when the shorter code exists and the longer does not.

Running this from your own disk: MATCH, the index, the lists and every cross-reference work with no network and no key. The links out to Wikipedia and Wikidata, and the READ button, are the only things that need a connection.

MATCH is lexical: it reads the words of your text against the words of the glosses, requires them to sit close together, and ranks tale types by shared motifs, title words and the vocabulary found in real tales of that type. It does not understand anything, and it says nothing when nothing in the text uses the index's vocabulary. That refusal is the feature.
